name: Balengou
overview: In the majority in their area of the Ndé, the Balengou are linked to the Baleng, with whom they share political rites, and live in contact with the Bamena, Baïok, Bangwa, Bafang and Mbouda. The chiefdom, the notables and the social classes (royal family, blacksmiths, craftsmen) structure a society where ancestors are honoured and where the mbouob festival brings the community together.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, mixing with Bamena, Baïok, Bangwa, Bafang and Mbouda; all speak Balengou, and many also speak the neighbouring languages.
Marriages within and outside the group; formerly, people married among Balengou and parents arranged the unions.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The natives of Balengou were joined by the Tenge, who came from Bafang.
Having come from Baleng via the north (Bamena side), the group remains tied to the Baleng, with whom it shares many rites, notably for enthronement.
The Balengou are attached to their land, which is dotted with sacred places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Social classes (royal family, notables, blacksmiths, craftspeople) and age classes (youths, adults, elders).

The chief decides for everyone, but there are several levels: family, neighbourhood, village, community. A problem goes up from the head of the family to the neighbourhood chief, the notables and then the chief.
Succession is hereditary within families.
Experienced people take care of the burial of dignitaries, funeral lamentations, the preservation of bodies and childbirths.
Formerly, people bowed before the chief; today, children sometimes call their elders by name.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the man takes his wife to his family.

Formerly, circumcision came when the father saw the boy becoming a man; the girl spent a period of seclusion in a corner (ndja), washing and anointing herself, before being presented to the suitors' families.
People used to marry between 25 and 30 years old for men, around 18-20 years old for women.
Steps: meeting of the parents, engagement, bride price, customary marriage; the exchange of cola and raffia wine seals the union.
The kola nut, with its many lobes, evokes discretion and hospitality; wine is an oath before the two families and the ancestors. Oil, goats, sheep, wrappers and salt are also offered.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cults to God and the ancestors, often at the end of the year during family gatherings, or individually at any time, through the successor.
Sacred places (mvé) come into being by themselves: graves, houses, forests, sacred huts.
Birth perpetuates the family and the name; life is cyclical, and the elder who leaves descendants remains present through them.
Taboos: a married child does not sit on his parents' bed; one does not spend the night with one's spouse at the in-laws'; incest requires rites.
Taboos: insolence and disobedience towards elders; a man does not insult his wife in public; certain pieces (gizzard) were reserved for men.
Serious offences: murder, destruction of sacred places, relations with one's brother's wife, witchcraft; offenders were banished or placed in quarantine.
Divination: clairvoyance with or without a medium, chicken, word, cowries, tarantula.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Women cultivated; men built houses and fences, raised livestock and sold the produce.
The land belongs to the family, and symbolically to the chief.
The artisan groups (blacksmiths, weavers, potters) have almost disappeared: they produced bags, clothes, calabashes, machetes, knives, hoes, spears, dibbers.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly, a cotton loincloth for men, a short skirt for women, cotton and raffia fabrics.
Traditional medicine has declined greatly in the Ndé in favour of hospitals.
Beauty lies in welcome, truth, hospitality and cheerfulness; in a woman, zeal for work is the first beauty.
Courtship: cheerfulness, attentiveness, respect, dancing talent and services rendered to the girl's family (fetching water, splitting wood, carrying maize).

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: mangambeu, ngwa; instruments: balafon, gourd zither, tam-tam, tjetja.
Dances: meyeb, leale at major events, koungang at funerals.
Festival: the mbouob (named after a whitish kaolin), celebrated according to the season.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Particularity: widowhood lasts only three days, compared with seven to nine elsewhere.

sections.title: The names
items: Names are common to both sexes, but there are masculine and feminine titles.
For the first children, one thinks of the parents and grandparents, then of the family and friends.
One changes name on rising in society (titles of nobility), sometimes several times; people are referred to by their praise name.
The founding ancestor is called Tchana.

lessons.title: Who are the Balengou? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Balengou community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Balengou community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Balengou community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Balengou community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Balengou community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Balengou call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, mixing with the Bamena, Baïok, Bangwa, Bafang and Mbouda; all speak Balengou, and many also the neighbouring languages. • Marriages within and outside the group; in the past, people married among Balengou and parents arranged the unions. • The indigenous people of Balengou were joined by the Tenge, who came from Bafang. • Having come from Baleng by the north (Bamena side), the group remains linked to the Baleng, with whom it shares many rites, notably for enthronement.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their area of the Ndé, the Balengou are linked to the Baleng, with whom they share political rites, and live in contact with the Bamena, Baïok, Bangwa, Bafang and Mbouda. The chiefdom, the notables and the social classes (royal family, blacksmiths, craftsmen) structure a society where ancestors are honoured and where the mbouob festival brings the community together.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Balengou community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Balengou
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Balengou organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Balengou village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Balengou organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Balengou village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Social classes (royal family, notables, blacksmiths, craftsmen) and age classes (young people, adults, elders). • The chief decides for everyone, but there are several levels: family, neighbourhood, village, community. A problem goes up from the head of the family to the neighbourhood head, to the notables and then to the chief. • Succession is hereditary within families. • Experienced people handle the burial of dignitaries, funeral lamentations, preservation of bodies and childbirth. • In the past, people bowed before the chief; today, children sometimes call their elders by name.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Social classes (royal family, notables, blacksmiths, craftspeople) and age classes (youths, adults, elders). The chief decides for everyone, but there are several levels: family, neighbourhood, village, community. A problem goes up from the head of the family to the neighbourhood head, to the notables and then to the chief. Succession is hereditary within families.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Balengou, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Balengou
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Balengou, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Balengou.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Balengou, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Balengou.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: sweet potato, pistachio dishes (melon). • Drinks: raffia wine. • The land belongs to the family, and symbolically to the chief.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Balengou mainly eat sweet potato, pistachio-seed dishes. Traditional drinks: raffia wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Balengou: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Balengou
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Balengou welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Balengou family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Balengou welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Balengou family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Names are common to both sexes, but there are masculine and feminine titles. • For first children, one thinks of the parents and grandparents, then of family and friends. • One changes name when rising in society (titles of nobility), sometimes several times; people are referred to by their praise name. • Birth perpetuates the family and the name; life is cyclical, and the elder who leaves descendants remains present through them. • In the past, circumcision came when the father saw the boy becoming a man; the girl spent a period of seclusion in a corner (ndja), washing and anointing herself, before being presented to the suitors' families.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Names are common to both sexes, but there are masculine and feminine titles. For first children, parents and grandparents are thought of, then family and friends. People change names as they rise in society (titles of nobility), sometimes several times; people are referred to by their praise name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments

student.memo: Among the Balengou, traditional dances (meyeb, major events, funerals) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon, gourd zither, drum, tjetja. Festival(s): mbouob festival.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Balengou
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Balengou, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Balengou. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Balengou, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Balengou. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Women farmed; men built houses and fences, raised livestock and sold the produce. • The land belongs to the family, and symbolically to the chief. • The groups of craftsmen (blacksmiths, weavers, potters) have almost disappeared: they produced bags, clothes, calabashes, machetes, knives, hoes, spears, dibbers.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Women cultivated; men built houses and fences, raised livestock and sold the produce. The land belongs to the family, and symbolically to the chief.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Balengou's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Balengou
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Balengou, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Balengou. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Balengou, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Balengou. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of God and the ancestors, often at the end of the year at family gatherings, or individually at any time, through the successor. • Sacred places (mvé) come into being by themselves: graves, houses, forests, sacred huts. • Birth perpetuates the family and the name; life is cyclical, and an elder who leaves descendants remains present through them. • Taboos: a married child does not sit on his parents' bed; one does not spend the night with one's spouse at the in-laws'; incest requires rites. • Prohibitions: insolence and disobedience towards elders; a man does not insult his wife in public; certain pieces (gizzard) were reserved for men.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cults to God and the ancestors, often at the end of the year during family gatherings, or individually at any time, through the successor. The sacred places (mvé) arise of themselves: graves, houses, forests, sacred huts.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Balengou (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Balengou
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Balengou and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Balengou family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Balengou greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Balengou family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Balengou. • The founding ancestor is called Tchana. • Particularity: widowhood lasts only three days, compared with seven to nine elsewhere.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Balengou are the first steps towards communicating with the Balengou. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Balengou.
